workingTitle: A hidden companion may be an unusually heavy neutron star
publicationStatus: Peer-reviewed Science Advances paper published November 11, 2026
coreFacts: J0008+0128 contains a visible red giant and an unseen companion in an orbit of about 1,218 days with eccentricity near 0.1.
Combined spectroscopy and Gaia astrometry give the red giant a best-fit mass of 1.67 solar masses and the unseen companion a best-fit mass of 2.20 solar masses.
High-resolution spectroscopy shows no detectable light from a second ordinary star, supporting a compact-object interpretation.
The unseen object is most likely a massive neutron star, but a low-mass black hole or a more complex compact system is not decisively excluded.
Binary-evolution calculations did not reproduce the unusually wide, nearly circular system, leaving its formation history unresolved.

sources.label: National Astronomical Observatories, Chinese Academy of Sciences

sourceStatus: Peer-reviewed paper metadata and the authors' institution release read; critical measurements, inference, and caveats checked.
caveats: The companion is not directly detected as a neutron star.
The mass interval overlaps both very massive neutron stars and possible low-mass black holes.
The formation pathway remains unresolved because current binary-evolution simulations did not reproduce the system.
